summary: I think Duolingo feels more like a game than a serious language learning tool, which ain't what I personally need.
top_quotes: Duolingo be feeling like I'm playing a game, not really learning.
I tried to take Duolingo seriously, but it ain't hit like Babbel does.
Man, I just need something that feels more structured and real, like Babbel, you feel me?

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hey, what's up? I'm Marcus, good to be here.

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Alright, so I’m from Atlanta, born and raised. You know, I got into tech pretty early. Always liked messin’ with computers, so it was kinda natural to go into software engineering. I went to Georgia Tech, been working in the field since. I love what I do, but I’m always looking to learn more, that’s why I started with the language apps.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: Grew up in ATL, man. Southside, to be specific. It’s my home, through and through.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: It was dope, to be real. Got that mix of city life but also a tight community feel. You know, everybody knows everybody, and folks always got your back. Being in the South, we got that hospitality, but also, it's where so much culture and creativity come from. I'm proud of where I come from.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: I think the turning point was when I landed my first tech gig. It was a big deal, man. I got that offer letter and realized, like, this is it, this is what I’m gonna do. Took a lot of hard work to get there, but seeing it pay off was huge. Opened up a lot of opportunities.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Mainly 'cause it put me on a path I didn't even know was possible growing up. I mean, ain't nobody in my family worked in tech before. So getting that job was like breaking new ground. It gave me the confidence that I could really make something of myself in this field.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: Handled it by just grindin', you feel me? I put in overtime studying, making sure I knew my stuff. And when I got there, I just kept asking questions, learning from anybody who would teach me. It was all about staying humble and eager to learn.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, it’s all about growth, both personally and professionally. In tech, things change so fast, so I wanna stay on top of my game. And on a personal level, it’s about developing other skills, like learning a new language, traveling more, and just expanding my horizons.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: It's important 'cause I believe in not getting too comfortable. You know, life is more than just work, and I wanna make sure I’m living it to the fullest, seeing different places, meeting new people, and understanding different cultures. It keeps life exciting.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day? Probably starts with a solid workout, gets my mind right. Then, killing it at work, maybe solving a tricky problem or shipping some new code. After work, hanging with friends or just chillin’ at home, maybe playing some games or catching up on a show.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: It’s all about that balance, you know? If I feel like I’ve been productive but also got to relax and have some fun, that’s a good day to me. Plus, if I get to learn something new, even better.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I’m more of a logical thinker, so I try to weigh the pros and cons, you know? I’ll do some research, talk to people who might have insight, and then just kinda sit with it. Sometimes gut feelings come into play too, but I like to be informed.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: I’m definitely a planner, no doubt. I like having structure, knowing what’s coming up. But I’m flexible too—like, if something unexpected pops up, I’ll roll with it. But having a plan feels good.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Like, if I’m going on a trip, I’ll have my itinerary all set, you know flights, where I’m staying, things I wanna see. But if, say, someone I meet suggests something cool to do, I ain’t gonna miss out just 'cause it wasn’t in the plan. I guess I plan so I don’t have to stress if things change.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I try to think through the worst-case scenario. If I can handle that, then maybe it’s worth the risk. I’m not super risk-averse, but I’m careful, you know? Especially in tech, where things can be unpredictable. But sometimes you just gotta leap, knowing you’ve done your prep.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: So, I usually get up around 6:30, hit the gym, then maybe have a quick breakfast. I start work around 9, and it’s a lotta coding, meetings, the usual tech stuff. I like to take breaks to stretch and clear my head. After work, I might chill, work on personal projects, or catch up with friends. I usually try to get some language practice in too. Then, wind down with some music or a show before crashing.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: Definitely work, especially when we’re in crunch mode, you know how it is. Also, learning new tech can be draining 'cause it’s a lot to take in. But it’s like a good kind of tired, where you feel like you did something worthwhile.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I had more time to really dive into learning languages. I do my best, but sometimes work gets so hectic it’s hard to keep that consistency. Also, just more time for family and friends, you know? Balance is key.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Last year, it was definitely balancing work and life, especially with everything being remote. It was like, the boundaries between work and home just disappeared, you feel me? Had to really work on setting aside time for myself and not letting work creep into everything.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I started setting hard stop times for work and making sure I stuck to them. Also, scheduling time to relax, workout, or just chill with people. It helped keep things separate and not let one take over the other.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: Probably my mom and my younger brother. We been through a lot together, and they always got my back. My brother’s kinda like my best friend, and my mom, well, she’s just always got that wisdom when I need it.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: They’re strong, you know? Built on years of love and just being there for each other. We talk almost every day, support one another, and all that. It’s good to have folks who just get you.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, probably at home. Working from home means I’m here a lot, but I got my little setup that makes it enjoyable. If I’m not there, I might be at a local coffee shop or just out in the city.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: They feel comfortable, familiar. Home is where I can just be me, no need to put on for anybody, you know? And when I’m out, like at a coffee shop, I like the buzz and energy. It’s stimulating, gets me inspired sometimes.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: It’s all about the vibe. Home is personal, filled with things I love. Outside, it’s about the energy and just seeing people do their thing. Both give me different kinds of comfort.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: I usually turn to my mom first. She always got that perspective that helps. Or my brother, depending on what it’s about. I got a couple of good friends I trust too, who I know won’t judge and just listen.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: I’d say dealing with a big project at work that went sideways. We had some tech issues, and it just wasn't coming together. It was super stressful, felt like all eyes were on me to fix it.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It kinda shook my confidence for a minute. Made me question if I was doing enough or if I was the right fit for the role. But eventually, I pushed through it, learned from it, and moved on. Just had to remind myself of past wins.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I leaned heavily on my support system. Talked it out with my family and some colleagues who could relate. Also took a step back to chill and recharge, you know, clear my head before jumping back in. That and remembering it’s not the end of the world, just a hurdle.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: I like to step away, maybe go for a run or listen to music. Something to ease my mind. Also, breaking things down into smaller tasks so it doesn’t feel so big. And definitely talking it out helps too.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: In a few years, I’d like to be taking on bigger roles in tech, maybe even lead a project or team. More travel, seeing places I've only dreamed about. Hopefully, speaking a couple more languages fluently, just being more well-rounded, you know?

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I’d want more balance, really. Like, less stress and more joy in the everyday. Also, just having a bit more freedom with my time, to do things that matter to me personally, beyond just work.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, I mostly used textbooks and some online resources. I mean, they were alright, but it was kinda boring and hard to stay consistent. You know how it is, just reading and trying to memorize without much practice. So then I moved on to Babbel, which was way better structured for me.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: It was definitely the lack of engagement. Those textbooks just felt dry, like I wasn't really absorbing anything, just cramming vocab. It wasn’t interactive at all, and I need to be engaged, like with real conversation or something more dynamic.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: I remember once I tried to hold a basic conversation with someone in Spanish. Man, I froze up 'cause I couldn't recall half of what I learned. Real talk, it was embarrassing. I realized just memorizing wasn't cutting it, I needed real practice.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I actually heard about Duolingo from some friends who were using it. They were all hyped about how you could learn languages on your phone, so I figured I’d check it out.

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: I figured, why not? It was free, so there wasn't really anything to lose. Plus, folks kept saying it was fun and easy to use on-the-go. I mean, I’m always on my phone anyway, so I thought I’d give it a shot.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: So, last time I used it, I opened the app, and you know, it hit me with those colorful little lessons. I started with a Spanish session, which was cool at first. They had me matching words and filling in blanks, which felt like I was doing alright. But then it got to this point where it turned into more of a game with all these notifications and streaks. It kinda felt like I was hitting levels in a game rather than making real progress.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: I’d say the repetition. Going over the same words and phrases helps it stick. And the immediate feedback when you mess up is pretty helpful, like you know exactly what you got wrong right away.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Honestly, the gamification, man. It starts to feel less like learning and more like I’m just trying to win the app. Plus the way it sometimes doesn’t explain why something’s wrong, just marks it wrong, can be frustrating.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: The vibe it gives off, like, it feels too much like playtime, you know? Like, I can’t take it serious 'cause it's got too many distractions. It’s like if you use an app for learning, you want it to have that focus, but with Duolingo, I start zoning out.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: I remember one time, I was doing this lesson, and it kept marking what I thought were correct answers wrong. But instead of giving me any sort of lesson or explanation, it just moved on. I was like, 'How am I supposed to get better if you don't show me where I went wrong?' That's when it really hit that this app wasn’t aligning with how I learn.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, I do. Sometimes, I look up additional explanations online or use other resources like Babbel to reinforce what Duolingo’s lessons skim over. I hate feeling like I’m missing the ‘why’ behind things, so that helps a lot.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give me a better understanding, basically. I get the context and clearer explanations which helps it stick better. Duolingo might get the ball rolling, but those other resources fill in the gaps, making sure I really learn stuff, not just memorizing for a streak.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst case, you spend all this time on Duolingo and come out not really speaking or understanding the language. I mean, you could have all these points and streaks, but if you can't hold a simple convo, what's the point? That’d be a waste of time.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I’m hoping it helps me level up my skills, you know? Like, actually teach me, not just entertain me. I wanna see real progress, like understanding when to use certain grammar or vocab in real situations. That’s the dream.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: If I can recognize words and phrases when I hear them or read them outside the app, then I know it’s sticking. If I feel more confident in trying to have a basic conversation, that’s when I’d say it’s working.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I’d make it less about the streaks and points, and more about in-depth lessons. More explanations, more context, a bit of real-world application. Basically, just make it feel like learning, not leveling up.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: I’d want systems that integrate conversation practice better. Like, something that pairs learning with real-world applications, maybe connects learners for practice, or simulates real-life scenarios better.

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: Nah, I think we hit everything. Just keen on exploring more apps that can really teach, not just entertain, you know?

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, that's cool with me. Go ahead, just keep it true to what we talked about, alright?
